game.whyConflict: {num} can't go here — it clashes with the {num} in row {r}, column {c}. A digit may appear only once per row, column and box.
game.whyConflictX: {num} can't go here — it clashes with the {num} in row {r}, column {c}. A digit may appear only once per row, column, box and long diagonal.
game.whyWrong: No visible clash, but {num} isn't the digit for this cell — the puzzle would become unsolvable. Tip: use notes (N) to narrow the candidates.
tour.digits: Tap a cell, then a digit, or type it. With Digit-first input on in Settings, tap the digit first, then each cell it goes in.
tour.notes: Notes mode pencils in the candidates a cell could hold instead of placing a digit. Press it again (or N) to switch back.
tour.hint: Stuck? A hint shows the next logical move, step by step. Each one costs a little of your score.
tour.undo: Takes back your last move, as many times as you like. Redo puts it back.
tour.pause: Pause (P) stops the clock and covers the board. The arrow on the left leads back to the menu.
hint.panelDesc: Stuck? Press Hint (H) and this panel walks you through the next logical step, one deduction at a time.
hint.move.none: No further logical move found from here.
hint.wrong.name: Wrong digit
hint.wrong.desc: The {num} at R{row}C{col} is wrong. Every hint builds on the digits already on the board, so this one has to go before the next step can be worked out.

hint.move.hidden-pair.name: Hidden Pair

hint.move.naked-triple.name: Naked Triple

hint.move.hidden-triple.name: Hidden Triple

hint.move.naked-quad.name: Naked Quad
hint.move.naked-quad.desc: Four cells together hold only {digits}. Remove those digits from {count} other cell(s) in the unit.
hint.move.hidden-quad.name: Hidden Quad
hint.move.hidden-quad.desc: {digits} are locked to four cells of a unit, so their other candidates can be removed.
hint.move.x-wing.name: X-Wing

hint.move.swordfish.name: Swordfish

hint.move.jellyfish.name: Jellyfish

hint.move.xy-wing.name: XY-Wing
hint.move.xy-wing.desc: An XY-Wing forces {num} out of {count} cell(s) seen by both pincers.

academy.title: Sudoku Academy
academy.subtitle: The {n} techniques the analyzer uses — each with a real worked example
academy.tapHint: Tap a card to see it worked out
academy.footer: These are exactly the techniques the in-game analyzer uses. When you request a hint, it applies them from Basic to Expert and shows the same step-by-step deduction.
academy.tech.naked-single.lookFor: A cell where only one digit is a valid candidate — every other digit already appears in its row, column, or box.
academy.tech.naked-single.howItHelps: Place that single remaining candidate. No deduction needed; the answer is forced by elimination.
academy.tech.naked-single.spot:
Pick a cell in a crowded row, column or box.
Note which digits already sit in its row, column and box.
If only one digit is missing from them, it goes in the cell.
academy.tech.naked-single.why: Each digit appears once per row, column and box. When the cell already sees every other digit, nothing else can go there.
academy.tech.naked-single.tips:
With notes on, look for a cell holding a single note.
No single anywhere? Scan one digit at a time for a Hidden Single.
academy.tech.hidden-single.lookFor: Within a row, column, or box, a digit that can only fit in one cell — even if that cell has other candidates too.
academy.tech.hidden-single.howItHelps: The digit has nowhere else to go in that unit, so it must go there. Place it.
academy.tech.hidden-single.spot:
Pick a digit, ideally one that is already placed often.
In a row, column or box still missing it, rule out the cells that already see it.
If only one cell is left in that unit, the digit goes there.
academy.tech.hidden-single.why: Every row, column and box holds each digit exactly once. If only one cell in the unit can take it, that cell must.
academy.tech.hidden-single.tips:
The cell may have other candidates; what counts is that the digit has nowhere else in the unit.
Boxes are usually the quickest place to find one.
academy.tech.pointing.lookFor: Inside a box, all candidates for a digit lie on a single row or column.
academy.tech.pointing.howItHelps: The digit must land on that line within the box, so remove it from the rest of that row or column outside the box.
academy.tech.pointing.spot:
Pick a box and a digit it still needs.
Check whether all its candidates for that digit sit on one row or one column.
If so, remove the digit from the rest of that line, outside the box.
academy.tech.pointing.why: The box must hold the digit somewhere on that line, so the line gets its copy from inside the box. No other cell of the line can have it.
academy.tech.pointing.tips:
Two or three candidates can point; the move is the same.
The mirror image, a line confined to one box, is Box-Line Reduction.
academy.tech.box-line.lookFor: All candidates for a digit within a row or column are confined to a single box.
academy.tech.box-line.howItHelps: The digit must live in that line, so remove it from every other cell of that box.
academy.tech.box-line.spot:
Pick a row or column and a digit it still needs.
Check whether all its candidates for that digit fall inside one box.
If so, remove the digit from the rest of that box.
academy.tech.box-line.why: The line must hold the digit where it crosses the box, so the box's copy is on that line. The box's other cells can't have it.
academy.tech.box-line.tips:
It is Pointing turned around: here the line restricts the box.
Check lines that cross a box full of candidates.
academy.tech.naked-pair.lookFor: Two cells in the same unit that each hold exactly the same two candidates and no others.
academy.tech.naked-pair.howItHelps: Those two digits fill those two cells in some order. Remove both from every other cell in the unit.
academy.tech.naked-pair.spot:
Look for cells with exactly two candidates.
Find two of them in the same row, column or box with the same pair.
Remove both digits from every other cell of that unit.
academy.tech.naked-pair.why: The two cells take those two digits between them, in one order or the other. That leaves neither digit for the rest of the unit.
academy.tech.naked-pair.tips:
If the two cells share both a line and a box, clear the digits from both.
Pairs are easiest to see with all notes filled in.
academy.tech.hidden-pair.lookFor: Two digits that appear as candidates in exactly two cells of a unit, and nowhere else in it.
academy.tech.hidden-pair.howItHelps: Those two cells must hold those two digits, so all their other candidates can be removed.
academy.tech.hidden-pair.spot:
Pick a row, column or box.
For each digit, count the cells where it can go.
Find two digits that fit only in the same two cells.
Remove every other candidate from those two cells.
academy.tech.hidden-pair.why: Both digits must go somewhere in the unit, and only those two cells can take them. So the cells hold those two digits and nothing else.
academy.tech.hidden-pair.tips:
Other candidates hide the pair; count spots per digit, not per cell.
Once cleared, it becomes a Naked Pair, which may help the rest of the unit.
academy.tech.naked-triple.lookFor: Three cells in a unit whose combined candidates are exactly three digits (each cell holds two or three of them).
academy.tech.naked-triple.howItHelps: Those three digits are locked into those three cells. Eliminate them from every other cell in the unit.
academy.tech.naked-triple.spot:
In one unit, look for cells with two or three candidates.
Find three cells whose candidates together are only three digits.
Remove those three digits from every other cell of the unit.
academy.tech.naked-triple.why: Three cells limited to three digits must use all three of them. None is left for the rest of the unit.
academy.tech.naked-triple.tips:
No cell needs all three digits; pairs like AB, BC and AC also make a triple.
Look at the unit's cells as a group, not one at a time.
academy.tech.hidden-triple.lookFor: Three digits that appear only across three cells of a unit, and nowhere else in it.
academy.tech.hidden-triple.howItHelps: Those three cells must contain those three digits, so strip all their other candidates.
academy.tech.hidden-triple.spot:
Pick a row, column or box.
Find three digits that can only go in the same three cells.
Remove every other candidate from those three cells.
academy.tech.hidden-triple.why: Those three digits need three cells in the unit, and only these three can take them. Anything else in them is impossible.
academy.tech.hidden-triple.tips:
A digit needn't fit all three cells, only none outside them.
Every hidden set has a naked twin among the unit's other cells. Look for whichever is smaller.
academy.tech.naked-quad.lookFor: Four cells in a unit whose combined candidates are exactly four digits.
academy.tech.naked-quad.howItHelps: Those four digits are confined to those four cells. Eliminate them from all other cells in the unit.
academy.tech.naked-quad.spot:
In one unit, look for cells with two to four candidates.
Find four cells whose candidates together are only four digits.
Remove those four digits from every other cell of the unit.
academy.tech.naked-quad.why: Four cells limited to four digits use up all four. None is left for the other cells of the unit.
academy.tech.naked-quad.tips:
Quads are rare; check for pairs and triples first.
If the unit has few other empty cells, the matching hidden set is smaller and easier to see.
academy.tech.hidden-quad.lookFor: Four digits that appear only within four cells of a unit.
academy.tech.hidden-quad.howItHelps: Those four cells own those four digits, so all their other candidates can be removed.
academy.tech.hidden-quad.spot:
Pick a row, column or box with many empty cells.
Find four digits that can only go in the same four cells.
Remove every other candidate from those four cells.
academy.tech.hidden-quad.why: Those four digits need four cells in the unit, and only these four can take them. So no other digit fits there.
academy.tech.hidden-quad.tips: Every hidden set has a naked twin among the unit's other cells. Look for whichever is smaller.
academy.tech.x-wing.lookFor: A digit with exactly two candidate cells in each of two rows (or columns), all sharing the same two columns (or rows).
academy.tech.x-wing.howItHelps: The digit is forced into those two lines, so remove it from those columns (or rows) everywhere else.
academy.tech.x-wing.spot:
Pick a digit.
Find rows where it has exactly two spots.
Look for two such rows whose spots sit in the same two columns.
Remove the digit from the rest of those columns. It works the same with rows and columns swapped.
academy.tech.x-wing.why: Each row puts the digit in one of its two spots, and the rows can't use the same column. So both columns get their copy from these rows, and no other cell in them can have it.
academy.tech.x-wing.tips:
Two corners may share a box; what matters is exactly two spots in each base row.
One extra spot in a row? Look for a Finned X-Wing.
academy.tech.swordfish.lookFor: Like an X-Wing but across three rows (or columns), with all candidates spanning exactly three columns (or rows).
academy.tech.swordfish.howItHelps: The digit is locked into those three lines, so remove it from the crossing lines everywhere else.
academy.tech.swordfish.spot:
Pick a digit.
Find rows where it has two or three spots.
Look for three such rows whose spots all fall in the same three columns.
Remove the digit from the rest of those columns, or do the same with rows and columns swapped.
academy.tech.swordfish.why: The three rows need three copies of the digit, each in a different column, and only three columns are on offer. Those columns get all their copies from these rows.
academy.tech.swordfish.tips:
A row doesn't need all three columns; two spots in a row is fine.
If only two rows fit, it is an X-Wing.
academy.tech.jellyfish.lookFor: A four-line X-Wing: a digit across four rows (or columns) confined to the same four columns (or rows).
academy.tech.jellyfish.howItHelps: The digit is locked into those four lines, so remove it from the crossing lines everywhere else.
academy.tech.jellyfish.spot:
Pick a digit.
Find rows where it has two to four spots.
Look for four such rows whose spots all fall in the same four columns.
Remove the digit from the rest of those columns, or do the same with rows and columns swapped.
academy.tech.jellyfish.why: Four rows need four copies of the digit in four different columns, and only four are on offer. Those columns get all their copies from these rows.
academy.tech.jellyfish.tips:
Very rare; try X-Wing and Swordfish on the digit first.
If you spot a smaller fish on the digit, it makes the same removals.
academy.tech.xy-wing.lookFor: Three bivalue cells: a pivot (X, Y) sharing one candidate with each of two pincers (X, Z) and (Y, Z).
academy.tech.xy-wing.howItHelps: Whatever fills the pivot, one pincer becomes Z. Any cell seeing both pincers loses Z.
academy.tech.xy-wing.spot:
Find a cell with exactly two candidates, X and Y: the pivot.
Among the cells it sees, find one with X and Z and another with Y and Z: the pincers.
Remove Z from every cell that sees both pincers.
academy.tech.xy-wing.why: If the pivot is X, the XZ pincer must be Z; if it is Y, the YZ pincer must be Z. Either way one pincer holds Z, so a cell seeing both can't.
academy.tech.xy-wing.tips:
All three cells hold exactly two candidates, and the pivot has no Z.
If the pivot holds Z too, it is an XYZ-Wing.
academy.tech.xyz-wing.lookFor: Like an XY-Wing, but the pivot holds three candidates (X, Y, Z) and the two pincers are (X, Z) and (Y, Z).
academy.tech.xyz-wing.howItHelps: One of the three cells must be Z, so any cell seeing all three loses Z.
academy.tech.xyz-wing.spot:
Find a cell with exactly three candidates, X, Y and Z: the pivot.
Among the cells it sees, find one with X and Z and another with Y and Z.
Remove Z from every cell that sees all three.
academy.tech.xyz-wing.why: Whatever the pivot is, Z lands in one of the three cells: the pivot itself or a pincer. A cell seeing all three can't be Z.
academy.tech.xyz-wing.tips:
Cells that see all three sit in the pivot's box, in line with one pincer.
If the pivot has only X and Y, it is an XY-Wing, which can clear more cells.

hint.move.skyscraper.name: Skyscraper
hint.move.skyscraper.desc: {num} has only two spots in each of two lines, and one end of each lines up. One of the other two ends must be {num}, so it can be removed from {count} cell(s) that see both.
hint.move.two-string-kite.name: 2-String Kite
hint.move.two-string-kite.desc: {num} has two spots in a row and two in a column, and one end of each shares a box. One of the far ends must be {num}, so it can be removed from {count} cell(s) that see both.
hint.move.unique-rectangle.name: Unique Rectangle
hint.move.unique-rectangle.desc: Three corners of a rectangle hold only {digits}. If the fourth were one of them too, the puzzle would have two solutions, so remove {digits} from it.
hint.move.simple-coloring.name: Simple Coloring
hint.move.simple-coloring.desc: Follow {num} through cells where it has only two places, coloring them in two alternating colors: one color is {num}. That removes {num} from {count} cell(s).
academy.tech.skyscraper.lookFor: A digit with exactly two candidates in each of two rows (or columns), where one end of each shares a column (or row) and the other ends don't.
academy.tech.skyscraper.howItHelps: The aligned ends can't both be the digit, so one of the two other ends is. Any cell that sees both of those ends loses the digit.
academy.tech.skyscraper.spot:
Pick a digit.
Find two rows where it has exactly two spots.
Check that one spot of each row shares a column, and the other two don't.
Remove the digit from cells that see both of the unaligned spots.
academy.tech.skyscraper.why: The aligned spots share a column, so at most one of them is the digit. The row that misses out puts it on its other spot, so at least one unaligned spot holds it.
academy.tech.skyscraper.tips:
It works sideways too, with columns as the base.
If the other two ends line up as well, it is an X-Wing.
academy.tech.two-string-kite.lookFor: A digit with exactly two candidates in a row and exactly two in a column, where one end of the row and one end of the column sit in the same box.
academy.tech.two-string-kite.howItHelps: Those two ends share a box, so at most one is the digit. That puts the digit on one of the far ends, and any cell seeing both far ends loses it.
academy.tech.two-string-kite.spot:
Pick a digit.
Find a row and a column where it has exactly two spots each.
Check that one spot of the row and one of the column share a box, without being the same cell.
Remove the digit from the cell that sees both far ends.
academy.tech.two-string-kite.why: The two ends in the shared box can't both be the digit. So the row or the column uses its far end, and the cell seeing both far ends loses it.
academy.tech.two-string-kite.tips:
The cell to clear sits where one far end's row meets the other's column.
All four spots are different cells; the box only links them.
academy.tech.unique-rectangle.lookFor: Four cells forming a rectangle over two rows, two columns and two boxes, where three of them hold exactly the same two candidates.
academy.tech.unique-rectangle.howItHelps: A rectangle of the same two digits could swap freely, giving two solutions. A proper puzzle has one, so the fourth corner can't be either digit.
academy.tech.unique-rectangle.spot:
Look for cells with the same two candidates.
Find three of them on the corners of a rectangle over two rows, two columns and two boxes.
If the fourth corner holds either digit of the pair plus others, remove the pair's digits from it.
academy.tech.unique-rectangle.why: If the fourth corner took one of the pair, the two digits could swap around the rectangle and the puzzle would have two solutions. A proper puzzle has one, so that corner gets another digit.
academy.tech.unique-rectangle.tips:
The rectangle must span exactly two boxes; across four, the swap would clash inside a box.
It relies on the puzzle having one solution.
academy.tech.simple-coloring.lookFor: A chain of cells linked because a digit has only two spots in their row, column or box. Color them alternately in two colors.
academy.tech.simple-coloring.howItHelps: Exactly one color holds the digit. If two cells of one color see each other, that color is wrong. A cell that sees both colors can't hold the digit.
academy.tech.simple-coloring.spot:
Pick a digit.
Find a row, column or box where it has exactly two spots, and color them two colors.
From each colored cell, follow more such pairs, alternating colors, to build a chain.
Look for two cells of one color that see each other, or a cell that sees both colors.
academy.tech.simple-coloring.why: Along each link exactly one end is the digit, so one whole color is true and the other false. Two cells of one color in a unit would put the digit there twice, so that color is false; a cell seeing both colors always sees the digit.
academy.tech.simple-coloring.tips:
Color only through units with exactly two spots; a third spot breaks the chain.
Once one color is false, the digit goes in every cell of the other.

hint.move.finned-x-wing.name: Finned X-Wing
hint.move.finned-x-wing.desc: {num} almost forms an X-Wing across two lines, except for a fin: extra spots inside one box. Either the X-Wing holds or a fin cell is {num}, and either way {num} can be removed from {count} cell(s) of that box on the crossing lines.
hint.move.w-wing.name: W-Wing
hint.move.w-wing.desc: Two cells that don't see each other hold the same pair: {num} and one other digit. That other digit has only two spots in a row, column or box, and each cell sees one of them, so the two cells can't both be it. One of them is {num}, so it can be removed from {count} cell(s) that see both.
hint.move.bug-plus-one.name: BUG+1
hint.move.bug-plus-one.desc: Every empty cell has two candidates except this one, which has three. If it weren't {num}, every digit would have exactly two spots in each row, column and box, and the puzzle would have two solutions. So it must be {num}.
academy.tech.finned-x-wing.lookFor: An X-Wing that's nearly there: a digit in two rows (or columns) fits the same two columns (or rows), apart from a few extra candidates, the fin, all in one box.
academy.tech.finned-x-wing.howItHelps: Either no fin cell is the digit and the X-Wing works as usual, or one is and the rest of its box loses the digit. Either way, cells in the fin's box on the X-Wing's columns (or rows) lose it.
academy.tech.finned-x-wing.spot:
Find an X-Wing on a digit that almost fits: the base rows have extra spots, all in one box.
Check that the extra spots, the fin, share a box with one corner of the X-Wing.
Remove the digit only from cells in the fin's box that lie in an X-Wing column.
academy.tech.finned-x-wing.why: Either the fin holds the digit and clears its box, or it doesn't and the X-Wing stands, clearing its columns. So cells in the fin's box and on those columns lose the digit either way.
academy.tech.finned-x-wing.tips:
It works with rows and columns swapped too.
No extra spots at all? Then it is a plain X-Wing, which clears more.
academy.tech.w-wing.lookFor: Two cells with the same two candidates, X and Y, that don't see each other, and a row, column or box where X has only two spots, each seen by one of the cells.
academy.tech.w-wing.howItHelps: Those two spots can't both lose X, so the two cells can't both be X. One of them is Y, and any cell that sees both loses Y.
academy.tech.w-wing.spot:
Find two cells with the same two candidates, X and Y, that don't see each other.
Find a row, column or box where X has exactly two spots, each seen by one of the cells.
Remove Y from every cell that sees both cells.
academy.tech.w-wing.why: X takes one of the two spots, and the cell seeing that spot can't be X. So at least one of the two cells is Y, and a cell seeing both can't be.
academy.tech.w-wing.tips:
Try each digit of the pair as the link.
If the two cells see each other, it is just a Naked Pair.
academy.tech.bug-plus-one.lookFor: Late in the puzzle, every empty cell has exactly two candidates except one, which has three.
academy.tech.bug-plus-one.howItHelps: Find the digit in that cell that appears three times in its row, column and box. Without it, every cell could switch to its other candidate and the puzzle would have two solutions, so that digit goes in the cell.
academy.tech.bug-plus-one.spot:
Late in the puzzle, with all notes in, check that every empty cell has two candidates except one.
That cell has three; find which of its digits appears three times in its row, column or box.
Place that digit.
academy.tech.bug-plus-one.why: Without the extra digit, every digit still missing from a unit would have exactly two spots in it, and the cells could swap, giving two solutions. So the extra digit must go there.
academy.tech.bug-plus-one.tips: Check that your notes are complete first; one missing note can fake a BUG.
hint.move.finned-swordfish.name: Finned Swordfish
hint.move.finned-swordfish.desc: Across three lines, {num} almost forms a Swordfish, except for a fin: extra spots inside one box. Either the Swordfish holds or a fin cell is {num}, and either way {num} can be removed from {count} cell(s) of that box on the crossing lines.
academy.tech.finned-swordfish.lookFor: A Swordfish that's nearly there: a digit in three rows (or columns) fits the same three columns (or rows), apart from a few extra candidates, the fin, all in one box.
academy.tech.finned-swordfish.howItHelps: Either no fin cell is the digit and the Swordfish works as usual, or one is and the rest of its box loses the digit. Either way, cells in the fin's box on the Swordfish's columns (or rows) lose it.
academy.tech.finned-swordfish.spot:
Find a Swordfish on a digit that almost fits: the base rows have extra spots, all in one box.
Check that the extra spots, the fin, share a box with one of the Swordfish's columns.
Remove the digit only from cells in the fin's box that lie in a Swordfish column.
academy.tech.finned-swordfish.why: Either the fin holds the digit and clears its box, or it doesn't and the Swordfish stands, clearing its three columns. So cells in the fin's box and on those columns lose the digit either way.
academy.tech.finned-swordfish.tips:
It works with rows and columns swapped too.
Only two base rows? Then look for a Finned X-Wing.
hint.move.empty-rectangle.name: Empty Rectangle
hint.move.empty-rectangle.desc: In one box, {num} fits only on one row and one column. Outside the box, {num} has just two spots in a column (or row), one of them on that row (column). Go from the other spot across to the box's column (row): that cell can't be {num}, or the box would have no spot left for it. So {num} can be removed from {count} cell(s).
academy.tech.empty-rectangle.lookFor: A box where a digit's candidates all lie on one row and one column (an L or a plus, not a single line), and outside the box a column (or row) where the digit has exactly two spots, one of them on that row (or column).
academy.tech.empty-rectangle.howItHelps: Take the cell in the other spot's row (or column) that lines up with the box's column (or row). If it were the digit, the first spot would be too, and together they'd leave the box no place for it. So that cell loses the digit.
academy.tech.empty-rectangle.spot:
Pick a digit and find a box where its candidates sit on one row and one column only.
Find a column (or row) outside the box where the digit has exactly two spots, one on the box's row (or column).
From the other spot, go across to the box's column (or row): that cell loses the digit.
academy.tech.empty-rectangle.why: If that cell held the digit, the other spot couldn't, so the first spot would. One clears the box's row, the other its column, and every candidate in the box is on those two lines.
academy.tech.empty-rectangle.tips:
The box needs candidates on both of its lines; on one line only, it's a Pointing Pair.
With just two candidates in the box, the box is a strong link of its own, and the pattern works like a 2-String Kite.
hint.move.xy-chain.name: XY-Chain
hint.move.xy-chain.desc: A chain of cells with two candidates each, every one seeing the next and sharing a digit with it, starts and ends with {num}. If the first cell isn't {num}, it's its other digit, which forces the next cell to its other digit, and so on until the last cell is {num}. One of the ends is {num}, so it can be removed from {count} cell(s) that see both.
academy.tech.xy-chain.lookFor: A chain of cells with exactly two candidates each, where each cell sees the next and shares a candidate with it, and the first and last cells both hold the same digit Z.
academy.tech.xy-chain.howItHelps: If the first cell isn't Z, every cell down the chain is forced to its other digit, and the last one is Z. So one end is Z, and any cell seeing both ends loses Z.
academy.tech.xy-chain.spot:
Pick a cell with two candidates and call one of them Z.
From its other digit, step to a cell it sees that holds that digit and one other, and go on from that other digit.
When a cell's other digit is Z, remove Z from every cell that sees both ends.
academy.tech.xy-chain.why: Suppose the first cell isn't Z. Then it's its other digit, so the next cell can't be that digit and must be its own other one, and so on to the last cell, which must be Z. Either the first cell or the last is Z, so a cell seeing both can't be.
academy.tech.xy-chain.tips:
An XY-Wing is the shortest XY-Chain, three cells long.
Every cell in the chain has exactly two candidates; a cell with three breaks it.

lesson.why.noDigit: That cell has no {d} pencil mark.

lesson.why.fishLines: This cell's row has {row} places for {d}, and its column {col}. This pattern needs lines with at most {k} places.
lesson.why.fishNone: Row {r} has {d} in columns {cols}, and column {c} in rows {rows}: no {n}-cell {technique} on {d} that clears anything goes through this cell.

lesson.why.noLink: Row {r} has {row} spots for {d}, and column {c} has {col}: neither line is a strong link, which needs exactly two.
lesson.why.skyLine.row: Row {r} has {d} in {n} places (columns {at}); this Skyscraper's rows need exactly two.
lesson.why.skyLine.col: Column {c} has {d} in {n} places (rows {at}); this Skyscraper's columns need exactly two.

lesson.why.erNone: In box {b}, {d} doesn't sit on just one row and one column, and neither row {r} nor column {c} has exactly two spots for it: this cell can't be part of any {technique}.
lesson.why.linkLine.row: Row {r} has {d} in {n} places (columns {at}); this {technique}'s link is a row with exactly two.
lesson.why.linkLine.col: Column {c} has {d} in {n} places (rows {at}); this {technique}'s link is a column with exactly two.
lesson.why.finLines: In row {r}, {d} is in columns {cols}; in column {c}, it's in rows {rows}. Neither line fits a {technique}: at most {k} spots, plus a fin inside one box.
lesson.why.notBase.row: In row {r}, {d} is in columns {at}: that row isn't one of this {technique}'s base rows.
lesson.why.notBase.col: In column {c}, {d} is in rows {at}: that column isn't one of this {technique}'s base columns.
lesson.why.wingMarks: That cell has {n} candidates; every cell of an XY-Wing has exactly two.
lesson.why.xyzMarks: That cell has {n} candidates; an XYZ-Wing's pivot has three and its pincers two.
lesson.why.noPincers: That cell holds {marks}, but no two cells it sees could be its pincers: two-candidate cells sharing one digit, holding those three between them.
lesson.why.notPivot: That cell doesn't see the pivot in row {pr}, column {pc}.
lesson.why.notAmong: Its candidates aren't all among the pivot's ({marks}) in row {pr}, column {pc}.
lesson.why.noShare: It shares no candidate with the pivot in row {pr}, column {pc}.
lesson.why.samePair: It holds the same two candidates as the pivot in row {pr}, column {pc}, so it can't be a pincer.
lesson.why.wNoX: That cell has no {x} mark, and every cell of this W-Wing has one.
lesson.why.wNoLink: That cell isn't one holding just {x} and {y}, and its row, column and box each have other than two spots for {x}, so no strong link on {x} runs through it.
lesson.why.chainNone: No {n}-cell XY-Chain on {z} that clears anything goes through that cell.
lesson.why.urMarks: That cell holds {marks}, not just {x} and {y}.
lesson.why.bugTwo: That cell has two candidates, like nearly every other. Look for the one with three.
lesson.why.inPattern: That mark is part of the pattern itself.
lesson.why.onlyRemoves: This move only removes {marks}, so the {num} mark stays.
lesson.why.seesOne: This cell sees the cell in row {r}, column {c} but not the one in row {mr}, column {mc}, so {d} can still go here.
lesson.why.seesNone: This cell sees neither the cell in row {r}, column {c} nor the one in row {mr}, column {mc}, so {d} can still go here.
lesson.why.offCover.row: Only columns {cover} lose {d}, outside the base rows; this cell isn't in them.
lesson.why.offCover.col: Only rows {cover} lose {d}, outside the base columns; this cell isn't in them.
lesson.why.offFin.row: Only cells in both box {b} and columns {cover} lose {d}; this one isn't.
lesson.why.offFin.col: Only cells in both box {b} and rows {cover} lose {d}; this one isn't.
lesson.why.seesOneSet: This cell doesn't see both sets of the chain, so {d} can still go here.
lesson.why.offUnit.row: Only the rest of row {n} loses {marks}; this cell isn't in it.
lesson.why.offUnit.col: Only the rest of column {n} loses {marks}; this cell isn't in it.
lesson.why.offUnit.box: Only the rest of box {n} loses {marks}; this cell isn't in it.

basics.prompt: New to sudoku? Learn to play in 2 minutes
basics.desc: Four short lessons: the rule, pencil marks, and the two simplest ways to find a digit.
basics.task.row: Every row holds the digits 1 to 9, each exactly once. Which digit is missing from this row?
basics.task.col: Every column follows the same rule. Which digit is missing here?
basics.task.box: And so does every 3×3 box. Which digit is missing from this box?
basics.task.notes: Not sure yet? Pencil it in. Turn on Notes (N), then write every digit that could still go in the green cell.
basics.task.single: Every empty cell shows its pencil marks. One cell has only one mark left: find it and write that digit in.
basics.task.scan: Wherever {d} already stands, it rules out its whole row and column (the dashed lines). Where can {d} go in the top-left box?
basics.notesFirst: Turn on Notes first (N, or the Notes button): pencil marks are for maybes.
basics.notesSoFar: Yes, {d} could go here. Any more?
basics.notesAll: That's all of them: {digits}. Only one is right, and the rest of the puzzle will tell you which.
